title: Mirtazapine and Alcohol: Sedation, Blackouts, and Safe Timing
excerpt: Can you drink on mirtazapine (Remeron)? How the sedating antidepressant and alcohol stack impairment, why blackouts happen, how timing works, and warning signs.
metaDescription: Can you drink on mirtazapine (Remeron)? How it stacks with alcohol, why blackouts happen, whether one drink is okay, and warning signs to watch for.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** mirtazapine (brand name Remeron) and alcohol are a poor combination, and the drug's US prescribing information tells patients to avoid alcohol. Mirtazapine is one of the most sedating antidepressants in common use, and alcohol is a sedative too. The label notes that the impairment in thinking and coordination from mirtazapine adds to the impairment from alcohol. In practice that means much heavier drowsiness, worse coordination, more memory gaps, and a higher risk of falls and accidents than you'd expect from the same number of drinks on a normal night. Alcohol also tends to worsen depression and sleep, which are usually the reasons someone is on mirtazapine in the first place. This guide explains how the two interact, why people report blackouts on surprisingly little alcohol, how timing works with a drug that stays in your body for days, and which warning signs mean you should get help.

**The quick rules:** Treat the label's advice to avoid alcohol as the default until your prescriber tells you otherwise. Don't take mirtazapine after a night of drinking without a plan you've agreed with your prescriber in advance. Don't stop mirtazapine suddenly just so you can drink. Never drive after combining the two. If someone is very hard to wake, breathing slowly or irregularly, or confused after mixing them, call 911 (or your local emergency number) right away.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and drug-label guidance. It is not a substitute for the doctor or pharmacist who prescribed your mirtazapine and knows your health history, dose, and other medicines. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist if** you take mirtazapine and drink regularly, you want to know whether any amount of alcohol is okay for you, you take other sedating medicines (sleep aids, anxiety medicines, opioid painkillers, antihistamines, gabapentin), or you take another antidepressant. **Get emergency help (call 911) if** someone who mixed mirtazapine and alcohol is hard to wake, breathing slowly, fainting, having a seizure, or very confused. If you're having thoughts of harming yourself, call or text 988 (the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline in the US) any time.

## What Mirtazapine (Remeron) Is

Mirtazapine is a prescription antidepressant. It was approved by the FDA in 1996 to treat major depressive disorder and is sold under the brand name Remeron, plus an orally disintegrating version called RemeronSolTab. Today most people take a generic. It's usually taken once a day at bedtime.

It belongs to a small class sometimes called NaSSAs, short for noradrenergic and specific serotonergic antidepressants. That's a mouthful, but it mainly tells you that mirtazapine works differently from the most common antidepressants, the SSRIs like sertraline (Zoloft) and escitalopram (Lexapro). It doesn't block serotonin reuptake. Instead, it blocks certain receptors that act as brakes on the release of serotonin and norepinephrine, and blocks a couple of serotonin receptors that are linked to side effects like nausea and sexual problems.

Doctors also prescribe it off-label in a few situations where its side effects are actually useful:

- **Trouble sleeping**, especially when insomnia comes with depression or anxiety.
- **Poor appetite or weight loss**, since mirtazapine commonly increases appetite.
- **People who couldn't tolerate SSRIs** because of nausea or sexual side effects.

That off-label use for sleep matters here. Like trazodone, mirtazapine is often thought of as "the pill that helps me sleep" rather than as a serious medicine, and that's when the alcohol warning gets overlooked. If you take trazodone instead, our [trazodone and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/trazodone-and-alcohol) covers that drug specifically.

### Why mirtazapine makes you so sleepy

Mirtazapine is a very strong blocker of **histamine H1 receptors**. Histamine is one of the brain's main "stay awake" signals, and blocking it is the same basic effect that makes diphenhydramine (Benadryl) drowsy, only mirtazapine's effect is considerably more potent.

An interesting quirk: many clinicians describe mirtazapine as **more sedating at lower doses** (such as 7.5 mg or 15 mg) than at higher doses. The usual explanation is that at low doses the antihistamine effect dominates, while at higher doses its norepinephrine-boosting effect partly offsets the sleepiness. That's one reason low doses are popular for sleep. It also means that "I'm only on a small dose" is not a reason to assume alcohol will be fine. The small dose may be the most sedating one.

## How Mirtazapine and Alcohol Interact: The Mechanism in Plain Words

There are three main ways the two clash. The first is by far the most important.

### 1. Stacked impairment and sedation (the biggest issue)

Alcohol is a central nervous system depressant. It slows brain activity mainly by boosting the brain's main calming signal (GABA) and dampening its main excitatory one (glutamate). Mirtazapine slows things down through a different route, mostly that strong antihistamine effect.

Different pathways, same destination: drowsiness, slower reactions, poor coordination, and fuzzy judgment. The US prescribing information for Remeron describes a small study in healthy men in which alcohol barely changed the amount of mirtazapine in the blood, but the impairment of thinking and motor skills from the two was additive. The label's conclusion is direct: patients should be advised to avoid alcohol while taking it.

That detail is worth pausing on. The interaction isn't mainly about one drug changing how the other is processed. It's about the effects piling up in your brain. So you can't "out-metabolize" it, and drinking water or eating doesn't cancel it.

At ordinary doses this mostly shows up as feeling far drunker and sleepier than usual, being unsteady on your feet, and slurring or losing track of conversations. At higher amounts of alcohol, or with other sedatives involved, the concern becomes slowed breathing and being hard to wake. Mirtazapine taken alone is generally considered less dangerous in overdose than older antidepressants, but serious outcomes become more likely when it's combined with alcohol or other sedating drugs.

### 2. Dizziness, low blood pressure, and falls

Mirtazapine commonly causes dizziness, and it can sometimes cause a drop in blood pressure when you stand up. Alcohol widens blood vessels and, through dehydration, lowers the fluid in your circulation. Put the two together with heavy drowsiness and you get the classic scenario: getting up in the night to use the bathroom, losing your balance, and falling. Falls are one of the most practical, real-world risks of this combination, especially for older adults.

### 3. Alcohol works against what mirtazapine is treating

Even when nothing dramatic happens, alcohol undermines the medicine:

- **Mood.** Alcohol acts as a depressant on mood as well as on the brain. Regular drinking is linked to worse depression and anxiety, and it can make it hard for you and your doctor to tell whether mirtazapine is working.
- **Sleep.** Alcohol can help you fall asleep faster, but as your body clears it in the second half of the night, sleep becomes lighter and more broken, and early-night REM sleep is suppressed. Our guide to [alcohol and REM sleep](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-rem-sleep-complete-scientific-analysis-2025) explains this in detail. On mirtazapine, that can mean a heavy knockout followed by a restless early morning and a very groggy day.
- **Appetite and weight.** Increased appetite and weight gain are among mirtazapine's most common side effects. Alcohol adds calories and tends to loosen restraint around late-night food. If weight gain on mirtazapine already bothers you, regular drinking makes it harder to manage.

## Mirtazapine, Alcohol, and Blackouts

Many people searching this topic are doing so because something already happened: they had a few drinks on mirtazapine and lost chunks of the evening, or woke up not remembering how they got home.

Here's why that happens. An alcohol **blackout** is a gap in memory caused by alcohol interfering with the brain's ability to store new memories, especially in the hippocampus, the area that turns short-term experiences into lasting ones. Blackouts are most closely tied to how high and how fast your blood alcohol rises. Sedating medicines that add to alcohol's impairment make it easier to cross that line, because your brain is already running at reduced capacity.

So a mirtazapine blackout isn't usually a sign of a rare reaction. It's what additive impairment looks like from the inside: the number of drinks that would normally leave you tipsy now produces the memory effects of a much heavier night. Other people may not even realize how impaired you are, because blackout drinkers can still walk and talk.

What to take from that:

- **Treat a blackout on mirtazapine as a clear warning sign** that the combination is affecting you strongly. It's worth telling your prescriber, without embarrassment. They hear this often.
- **The next-day risk doesn't end at memory.** People in a blackout are more likely to fall, get hurt, make unsafe decisions, or be unable to protect themselves.
- **If you're with someone who seems far more impaired than their drinks would explain,** don't leave them alone, don't let them drive, and watch their breathing.

For more on what blackouts are and why they happen, see our guide on [blackout drinking](/never-hungover/blackout-drunk).

## What the Label and Official Guidance Say

The guidance here is unusually clear for a medication question:

- **The US prescribing information** describes the additive impairment of cognitive and motor skills with alcohol and states that patients should be advised to avoid alcohol while taking mirtazapine. It also warns about combining it with other sedatives such as benzodiazepines, and cautions against driving or operating machinery until you know how the drug affects you.
- **Pharmacy labels and patient leaflets** typically say to avoid alcohol and warn that the medicine may cause drowsiness.
- **Mirtazapine carries the FDA boxed warning shared by all antidepressants** about increased risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviors in children, teens, and young adults, particularly when starting treatment or changing the dose. Alcohol lowers inhibition and can worsen mood, which is one more reason the combination deserves care.

What you won't find is an official "safe number of drinks" on mirtazapine. The risk depends on your dose, your age, your body, your other medicines, and what you're doing afterward. That's a conversation for your prescriber.

## Remeron and Alcohol: Is the Brand Any Different?

No. Remeron is the original brand name for mirtazapine, and RemeronSolTab is the orally disintegrating tablet that melts on the tongue. Generic mirtazapine tablets and disintegrating tablets contain the same active ingredient. The alcohol advice is identical for all of them.

One small practical difference: the disintegrating version is sometimes used by people who have trouble swallowing pills. It's no faster or safer with alcohol. The disintegrating tablets also contain phenylalanine, which matters only for people with the genetic condition phenylketonuria (PKU).

## Can You Have One Drink on Mirtazapine?

This is the question most people actually want answered, and the honest answer is: **it depends, and your prescriber is the right person to decide.**

How to think about it:

- **The official advice is to avoid alcohol.** Even one drink adds to mirtazapine's sedation.
- **Some prescribers are comfortable with occasional light drinking** for some patients who are stable on their dose, for example a single drink with an early dinner several hours before a bedtime dose. Others recommend no alcohol, particularly for people with depression, older adults, people who have had falls, and people on other sedating medicines.
- **Mirtazapine's long half-life changes the math.** Unlike shorter-acting sleep medicines, a nightly dose of mirtazapine means some of the drug is always in your system (more on that below). So even a drink in the afternoon overlaps with it to some extent.
- **The first weeks are the riskiest time to experiment.** Sedation is often strongest when you first start mirtazapine or change the dose, before your body adjusts.

If your prescriber has given the okay for occasional light drinking, these habits keep the risk lower:

- Keep it to one drink, with food, early in the evening.
- Know how your usual dose affects you before you add anything.
- Don't drive, and plan to stay in for the night.
- Get up slowly if you wake in the night: sit on the edge of the bed for a moment before standing.

If you haven't asked, assume the answer is "avoid it" until you do.

## I Already Drank. Should I Take My Mirtazapine Tonight?

This is the most common real-life situation, and it's much better to have the answer before the night happens. **Ask your prescriber ahead of time what they want you to do on a night you've been drinking.** The right answer varies, which is why a blanket rule here isn't possible.

Some general points that apply to most people:

- **Don't take extra or a "make-up" dose** the next night to compensate for anything.
- **Don't take it while you're still clearly drunk** to help you "sleep it off." Adding a strong sedative on top of a lot of alcohol makes oversedation, vomiting while drowsy, and falls more likely.
- **Skipping a single dose is usually not dangerous** for most people, though you may sleep worse. Because mirtazapine lasts a long time in the body, one missed dose doesn't drop your level to zero. But if you take it for depression, repeatedly skipping doses around drinking is not a good plan for your treatment.
- **Don't swap in another sleep aid** like diphenhydramine, doxylamine, or melatonin. Those have their own problems with alcohol and with mirtazapine. Our guides on [melatonin and alcohol](/never-hungover/melatonin-and-alcohol) and [Benadryl for hangovers](/never-hungover/benadryl-for-hangover) explain why.

If you can't sleep after drinking without your usual medicine, our article on [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking) explains what's going on and what tends to help.

## How Long Does Mirtazapine Stay in Your System?

This is where mirtazapine differs most from shorter-acting sleep medicines. Its half-life (the time it takes for the level in your blood to fall by half) is commonly reported at roughly **20 to 40 hours** in adults. It tends to be longer in older adults, in women, and in people with reduced liver or kidney function.

A rough rule of thumb in pharmacology is that a drug is mostly cleared after about five half-lives. For mirtazapine, that works out to several days, and possibly a week or more for some people.

What that means in practice:

- **If you take mirtazapine every night, there is always some in your system.** There's no window during the day when it's "worn off."
- **Waiting a few hours after your dose doesn't make drinking safe.** The question isn't really "how long after mirtazapine can I drink," it's "should I drink at all while I'm on it." That's one for your prescriber.
- **After you stop mirtazapine** (with your doctor's guidance), it still takes several days for it to leave your system. If you're stopping and want to know when alcohol is less of a concern, ask your prescriber or pharmacist.

## How Long After Drinking Can You Take Mirtazapine?

There's no official waiting period that applies to everyone, and anyone who gives you an exact number of hours is guessing. What you can say:

- **Your body clears roughly one standard drink per hour,** though this varies with body size, sex, food, and genetics. After a heavy night, alcohol can still be in your blood the next morning.
- **The goal is to avoid peak alcohol and a fresh dose landing at the same time.** One drink with an early dinner and a late bedtime dose is a very different situation from several drinks right before bed.
- **Because mirtazapine is always on board for nightly users,** the safest approach is to agree a plan with your prescriber rather than calculating hours on your own.

## Mirtazapine, Alcohol, and the Next Morning

Many people already feel a "mirtazapine hangover" without alcohol: grogginess, heavy limbs, and slow thinking for the first few hours of the day, especially early in treatment. Add alcohol and the next morning often feels considerably worse:

- **Leftover sedation** from mirtazapine's long action.
- **A regular hangover:** dehydration, broken sleep in the second half of the night, low blood sugar, and an irritated stomach.
- **Dizziness on standing,** from mirtazapine plus dehydration.
- **Dry mouth and headache,** which both substances can cause.
- **Low mood or anxiety the day after drinking,** which can feel especially heavy if you're being treated for depression. Our guide to [hangxiety](/never-hungover/hangxiety-complete-guide-2026-supplements-research) explains why mood dips after drinking.

What helps: drink water steadily, eat something simple, get up slowly, and don't drive until you feel fully clear. Impairment from sedating medicines can last longer than you feel it does. If the dizziness is severe, you faint, or you can't shake the confusion, get medical help rather than waiting it out.

## Other Medicines That Make the Combination Riskier

The mirtazapine-plus-alcohol risk rises quickly when a third sedating or serotonin-affecting drug is involved. Tell your prescriber and pharmacist about everything you take, including over-the-counter products and supplements.

| Type of medicine | Examples | Why it matters with mirtazapine and alcohol |
|---|---|---|
| Benzodiazepines and sleep drugs | alprazolam (Xanax), lorazepam (Ativan), diazepam (Valium), zolpidem (Ambien) | Three sedatives stacked; higher risk of oversedation and slowed breathing |
| Opioid painkillers | oxycodone, hydrocodone, codeine, tramadol | Strong combined sedation and breathing suppression; tramadol also adds serotonin risk |
| Gabapentinoids | gabapentin, pregabalin | Added sedation, dizziness, and breathing risk |
| Sedating antihistamines | diphenhydramine, doxylamine (in many "PM" and night-time cold products) | Added drowsiness and confusion |
| Other antidepressants and serotonin drugs | SSRIs, SNRIs, trazodone, triptans, St. John's wort | Small risk of serotonin syndrome; mirtazapine is sometimes prescribed alongside an SSRI, which is fine under supervision but adds complexity |
| Drugs that raise mirtazapine levels | some antifungals (like ketoconazole), some HIV medicines, clarithromycin, cimetidine | Higher mirtazapine levels mean stronger sedation |

If you take Xanax or a similar medicine, our [Xanax and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/xanax-and-alcohol) explains why that particular combination is especially risky. For a broader look at alcohol and antidepressants as a group, see our [antidepressants and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/antidepressants-and-alcohol).

**Serotonin syndrome** is uncommon but worth recognizing. Signs include agitation, confusion, sweating, shivering, a fast heart rate, muscle twitching or stiffness, fever, and diarrhea. It needs urgent care.

## Who Should Be Most Careful

You're at higher risk from mixing mirtazapine and alcohol if you:

- **Are 65 or older.** Mirtazapine tends to stay in the body longer, and older adults are more sensitive to sedation and more likely to fall and be badly hurt.
- **Take mirtazapine for depression,** especially if you've had thoughts of self-harm. Alcohol worsens mood and lowers inhibition.
- **Recently started mirtazapine or changed your dose.** Sedation is usually strongest at this stage.
- **Take other sedating medicines,** as listed above.
- **Have liver or kidney disease,** which can raise mirtazapine levels.
- **Have sleep apnea.** Alcohol and sedating medicines can relax the airway and make breathing pauses worse.
- **Drink most days or binge.** The more often and heavily you drink, the more often the two overlap.

If any of these apply, ask your prescriber directly about alcohol.

## Warning Signs: When to Get Help

Most people who drink on mirtazapine will just feel very drowsy, unsteady, and foggy. But some situations are emergencies. **Call 911 (or your local emergency number) if someone who has mixed mirtazapine and alcohol:**

- Can't be woken up, or is very hard to wake
- Is breathing slowly, shallowly, or irregularly, or has blue-tinged lips
- Faints, or has a racing, pounding, or irregular heartbeat
- Has a seizure
- Is very confused, agitated, feverish, or has muscle stiffness or twitching (possible serotonin syndrome)
- Took more mirtazapine than prescribed, or took it with other sedatives

While you wait, don't leave the person alone. If they're drowsy, lay them on their side so they won't choke if they vomit. In the US you can also call Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222** if you're unsure whether something needs the emergency room.

**Two mirtazapine-specific warnings worth knowing** (not caused by alcohol, but easy to confuse with a bad hangover):

- **Fever, sore throat, mouth sores, or flu-like signs of infection.** Mirtazapine can, rarely, lower white blood cell counts. If you develop these symptoms, contact your doctor promptly so they can check.
- **Unusual confusion, headache, weakness, or unsteadiness that doesn't fit your drinking.** Mirtazapine, like other antidepressants, can occasionally cause low sodium levels, which is more likely in older adults. Heavy drinking can also disturb sodium. These symptoms are worth a medical check.

**And if your mood is the issue:** if your depression is getting worse or you're having thoughts of harming yourself, call or text **988** in the US. That's true whether or not alcohol is involved.

## Don't Stop Mirtazapine Just to Drink

Some people decide to skip their medicine for a few days around a wedding, a holiday, or a vacation. It's understandable, but it doesn't work well with mirtazapine. Because the drug lasts so long in the body, a couple of skipped days won't clear it before the event. And stopping suddenly, especially after weeks or months of use, can cause discontinuation symptoms such as dizziness, nausea, anxiety, agitation, trouble sleeping, and vivid dreams. If you take it for depression, gaps in treatment can also let symptoms creep back.

If alcohol and your medicine keep clashing, bring it up with your prescriber. They may suggest a different plan for occasions, adjust the dose or timing, or talk through other options.

## Sleeping Better Without Leaning on Alcohol

If you're on mirtazapine partly for sleep, it's worth knowing that alcohol is one of the most common hidden causes of poor sleep. It makes you drowsy at first, as our guide on [why alcohol makes you sleepy](/never-hungover/why-does-alcohol-make-you-sleepy) explains, then fragments the second half of the night. Many people find their sleep improves simply by keeping alcohol lighter and earlier. Our guide to [sleep optimization for social drinkers](/never-hungover/sleep-optimization-social-drinkers-circadian-rhythm) covers practical habits. Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is the first-line treatment recommended by major sleep medicine groups, and it's worth asking about if you've relied on a sedating medicine for a long time.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

Some readers who drink socially ask about DHM (dihydromyricetin), a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that's sold as a hangover supplement. Here's the honest picture:

- Research on DHM comes mostly from animal and lab studies, including work suggesting it affects how the brain responds to alcohol and supports alcohol metabolism. Human evidence is limited.
- **There is no good evidence that DHM makes it safe to combine mirtazapine and alcohol.** It doesn't cancel out sedation, it doesn't prevent blackouts, and it's not a reason to drink on mirtazapine.
- DHM may have its own effects on brain GABA signaling, and it hasn't been studied alongside mirtazapine. **If you take mirtazapine or any other prescription medicine, ask your doctor or pharmacist before adding DHM.** Our [medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers what's known.

If you're not on sedating medicines and you're simply looking for something to support a night out, our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how people typically use it, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. A widely used option is [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20); a higher-priced combination formula is [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20). Neither replaces the basics in our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover): drinking less, drinking slower, eating, and staying hydrated.

## The Bottom Line

- Mirtazapine is a strongly sedating antidepressant, and its label says to avoid alcohol because the impairment from the two adds together.
- Low doses can be the most sedating, so a small dose isn't a reason to assume drinking is fine.
- Blackouts on a few drinks are a known consequence of stacked impairment, and a sign to talk to your prescriber.
- Mirtazapine's half-life of roughly 20 to 40 hours means nightly users always have some on board. Waiting a few hours doesn't make drinking safe.
- Agree a plan with your prescriber for nights you drink, and don't stop the medicine suddenly to make room for alcohol.
- Call 911 for anyone who is hard to wake, breathing slowly, fainting, or having a seizure after mixing the two.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking mirtazapine?**

The official guidance is to avoid it. Mirtazapine's US label says the impairment in thinking and motor skills from mirtazapine adds to the impairment from alcohol and advises patients to avoid alcohol. Together they can cause heavy drowsiness, poor coordination, memory gaps, and falls. Some prescribers allow occasional light drinking for certain stable patients, so ask yours what's appropriate for you.

**Is Remeron and alcohol different from generic mirtazapine and alcohol?**

No. Remeron and RemeronSolTab are brand names for mirtazapine, and generic versions contain the same active ingredient. The alcohol warning, the sedation risk, and the advice to talk to your prescriber are the same whichever version you take.

**Why did I black out after only a few drinks on mirtazapine?**

Mirtazapine is strongly sedating, and its effects add to alcohol's. Blackouts happen when alcohol interferes with the brain's ability to store new memories, and a sedating medicine makes it easier to reach that point on fewer drinks. A blackout on mirtazapine is a clear sign the combination is affecting you strongly, and it's worth telling your prescriber.

**Is one drink okay on mirtazapine?**

It might be for some people, but it's a decision to make with your prescriber. The label advises avoiding alcohol, low doses can be very sedating, and the first weeks of treatment are usually the most sedating. If you're older, take mirtazapine for depression, take other sedating medicines, or have had falls, your prescriber may advise no alcohol at all.

**How long after taking mirtazapine can I drink?**

Mirtazapine's half-life is commonly reported at roughly 20 to 40 hours, so if you take it nightly there's always some in your system. Waiting a few hours after your dose doesn't make drinking safe. The real question is whether any drinking is okay for you while you're on it, and that's one for your prescriber.

**Should I take my mirtazapine if I've been drinking?**

Ask your prescriber for a plan before it comes up, because the right answer depends on your dose and why you take it. Don't take it while you're still clearly drunk, and never take an extra dose to make up for a missed one. Missing a single dose is usually not dangerous because the drug lasts a long time, but repeatedly skipping doses isn't a good plan if you take it for depression.

**Can mirtazapine and alcohol kill you?**

It's possible, though uncommon. Mirtazapine on its own is generally considered less dangerous in overdose than older antidepressants, but serious outcomes become more likely when it's combined with large amounts of alcohol or other sedatives such as benzodiazepines or opioids. Falls and accidents are also real risks. If someone is hard to wake, breathing slowly, or unresponsive, call 911.

**Does mirtazapine make you more drunk?**

It can make you feel and act much more impaired. The Remeron label describes alcohol barely changing mirtazapine blood levels, but the two drugs' effects on thinking and coordination add together. So your blood alcohol may be the same as usual, while your coordination, judgment, and memory are worse than the same drinks would normally cause.

**Does DHM make it safe to drink on mirtazapine?**

No. There is no good evidence that DHM reduces the sedation, memory effects, or other risks of combining mirtazapine and alcohol, and DHM hasn't been studied alongside mirtazapine. If you take mirtazapine or any prescription medicine, ask your doctor or pharmacist before adding DHM or any other supplement.

faq.answer: No. There is no good evidence that DHM reduces the sedation, memory effects, or other risks of combining mirtazapine and alcohol, and DHM hasn't been studied alongside mirtazapine. If you take mirtazapine or any prescription medicine, ask your doctor or pharmacist before adding DHM or any other supplement.
